extracted.intended_audience: Firefox and Pocket users, publishers/creators, and readers interested in Pocket's recommendation approach
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and editorial criteria describing how Pocket (Mozilla) selects and surfaces recommended content for Firefox New Tab and Pocket users, including algorithmic signals and human curator practices. Covers what content is elevated, avoided, and how privacy and publisher diversity are treated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality-content bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Pocket editorial team works hard to maintain one bias: quality content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pocket prioritizes quality content over sensationalism or low-value items. This includes avoiding clickbait and misinformation, and elevating pieces believed to be "worthy of [readers'] time and attention."

rubrics_metrics.name: Human editor vetting / curation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations are vetted by thoughtful, dedicated human editors who do a lot of reading and watching so you don’t have to dig through the muck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithms surface candidate items but human curators sift through this material and elevate great reads (in-depth features, clever explainers, curiosity chasers, timely reads, evergreen pieces). Human judgement is central to final recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic signal: most-saved and most-read
rubrics_metrics.description: Pocket’s algorithms surface the most-saved and most-read content from the Pocket community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community saving and reading behavior form the foundation of what algorithms flag for curator consideration; saves are treated as a stronger, personal signal than simple likes or clicks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for in-depth / high-altitude pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: Pocket recommendations often have a wider or higher altitude view — not necessarily the first- or second-day story but the Sunday magazine story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer, more in-depth reads (features, explainers, context pieces) are preferred over immediate breaking-news snippets or shallow clickbait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of clickbait and sensational content
rubrics_metrics.description: Along with misinformation, you won’t find clickbait on Pocket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curators avoid recommending items whose primary purpose is to shock, bait engagement, or deploy tracking/ads rather than provide value. Example anti-pattern: "Here’s what 10 celebs look like in bikinis."

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of misinformation and poorly sourced claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Curators won’t recommend content they believe is misleading or sensational, or articles based on studies with just a single source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They prefer pieces corroborated by multiple sources and will wait until there is more information to confirm or debunk a story before recommending it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source integrity / publisher history
rubrics_metrics.description: Curators avoid recommending content from a source without a strong history of integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A source’s reputation and track record for accurate, trustworthy reporting is a factor in whether its pieces are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity and representation of publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: The curator team makes sure that a wide assortment of publishers are represented, as well as a large variety of topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pocket surfaces content from major outlets (NYT, Guardian, Wired) and smaller publications or indie web publishers, allowing diverse voices to get wider exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amplifying smaller publications / surfacing gems
rubrics_metrics.description: Pocket’s algorithms flag notable stories from smaller publications for curator consideration, enabling them to get wider exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pocket intentionally elevates exceptional content from small players and indie web publications, not just the usual suspects; this can drive significant traffic and audience growth for those publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for reader privacy (non-targeting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pocket respects and preserves the privacy of readers; it doesn’t mine everyone’s data to show creepily targeted stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations are not based on intensive personal data mining or creepy targeting; privacy is a design principle tied to Mozilla’s values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signal meaning: saving as a personal indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Saving something in your Pocket is different from pressing the 'like' button — it’s more personal and less performative, and often points to real gems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pocket treats saves as meaningful signals for future recommendation curation (users save for later rather than for immediate performative engagement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid baiting engagement / not designed to trap attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Pocket’s interface and recommendations aren’t designed to trap you or bring you down; they aren’t trying to shock or surprise people into clicking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and editorial choices aim to avoid addictive, attention-maximizing tactics; instead they offer content believed to be worthy of time and attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review of meta-image / preview visuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Curators review the meta-image (the preview image that appears when an article is shared) and take care to avoid surprising people with inappropriate visuals on the Firefox new tab.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since curators don’t control publisher-selected images, they screen and avoid recommending items whose preview images could be inappropriate or misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curated thematic collections to amplify voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Pocket publishes curated collections (e.g., Racial Justice collections) assembled by subject-matter curators like Black scholars, journalists and writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thematic collections are used proactively to amplify and champion specific voices and topics; curators may create collections to provide context and surface authoritative perspectives.
